Scurrilous

SKUR-uh-lus · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Scurrilous is slanderous and grossly abusive, typically making false accusations.

The rival campaign's scurrilous flyer accused the candidate of crimes with zero evidence attached.

Worked Example

The scurrilous unsigned letter spread false, ugly rumors about the new principal before she'd even started the job.

Scurrilous specifically describes abusive language that attacks someone's character, typically without proof.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

slanderous: A slanderous statement is a false spoken remark that damages someone's reputation -- the term points at one specific lie. Scurrilous describes the character of an entire assault on someone's name: coarse, mocking abuse piled on top of false accusations. One made-up rumor is slanderous; a pamphlet dripping with mockery and made-up misdeeds is scurrilous.

abusive: Abusive language is extremely harsh and insulting -- it wounds, but it may contain no claims at all, just venom, and it can even be true. Scurrilous language goes further in one particular way: the abuse carries false accusations meant to blacken someone's name. Screaming at a referee is abusive; spreading made-up scandals about him is scurrilous.

vulgar: Vulgar language is crude and indecent -- swearing and coarse jokes that offend good taste without accusing anyone of anything. Scurrilous language is aimed at a person: it abuses its target and typically makes false accusations. A comedian can be vulgar and harm no one's name; a scurrilous attack exists to ruin one.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

complimentary: expressing praise or admiration

respectful: showing deference and high regard

Where it sits · how damaging the false attack is — insulting → scurrilous → libelous

insulting vs. scurrilous: Insulting is a general word for offensive speech; scurrilous adds a specific sense of false, damaging attack.

libelous vs. scurrilous: Libelous goes further than scurrilous, specifically implying a false published statement that could be sued over.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — scurr

root — scurr: buffoon, jester (Latin (scurra))

suffix — -ilous

suffix — -ilous: full of, characterized by (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: scurr- (from scurra, 'buffoon' or 'jester') + -ilous together trace back to the crude, mocking humor of a jester -- now describing abusive, slanderous language.

Use the root in a new word: scurrility

Use the root in a new word: scurrility: Scurrility is the noun form of the same word family, naming abusive language itself.
